然而，在通常情况下，我们的防御机制使我们无法察觉无意识的体验，即使焦虑持续时间较长或反复出现，也无法突破我们的压抑。那么，在没有心理治疗的帮助下，我们如何才能了解自身无意识的运作方式呢？正如我之前提到的，如果我们能够识别出自身的行为模式，它们就能提供线索，尤其是在人际关系领域，特别是恋爱或性关系中，因为正是在这里……我们最初在家庭中未解决的冲突会重演。此外，如果我们懂得如何运用，就可以通过梦境和任何创造性活动来接触我们的潜意识，因为梦境和创造力，无论是否出于我们的意识意志或欲望，都直接源于潜意识。

Under ordinary circumstances, however, our defenses keep us unaware of our unconscious experience, and our anxiety, even if it is somewhat prolonged or recurrent, doesn’t succeed in breaking through our repression. How then, without the aid of psychotherapy, can we learn about the operations of our own unconscious? As I noted earlier, patterns in our behavior, if we can recognize them, provide clues, especially in the area of interpersonal relations and, within that domain, especially in our romantic or sexual relationships, because it is here that our initial unresolved conflicts within the family are reenacted. In addition, we have access to our unconscious, if we know how to use it, through our dreams and through any creative activities we engage in because both our dreams and our creativity, independent of our conscious will or desire, draw directly on the unconscious.

梦境和梦的象征意义

Dreams and dream symbols

人们认为，睡眠时我们的防御机制与清醒时不同。睡眠期间，潜意识可以自由表达，并在梦境中得以展现。然而，即使在梦境中，也存在某种审查机制，某种保护机制，防止我们触及那些压抑的经历和情绪中令人恐惧的真相，而这种保护机制以梦境扭曲的形式出现。潜意识在梦境中表达的“信息”，也就是梦境的潜在含义或潜在内容，会通过被称为置换和凝缩的过程发生改变，使我们难以识别。当我们用一个“安全”的人、事或物作为“替代品”来代表一个更具威胁性的人、事或物时，梦境置换就会发生。例如，我可能会梦见一位小学老师性侵我，以此来表达（同时也是为了逃避）我潜意识中知道的父母之一曾性侵我的事实。在梦境中，当我们用单一的梦境意象或事件来代表多个潜意识创伤或冲突时，就会发生凝缩现象。例如，我梦见自己与一头凶猛的熊搏斗，可能代表着我在家中和工作中遇到的心理“斗争”或冲突。或者，以上述例子为例，我梦见自己被小学老师性骚扰，可能代表着我潜意识里感到自己的自尊心正受到来自众多家庭成员、朋友和同事的攻击。（因此，单一的梦境事件可能同时是转移和凝缩的产物。）

When we sleep, it is believed that our defenses do not operate in the same manner as they do when we are awake. During sleep, the unconscious is free to express itself, and it does so in our dreams. However, even in our dreams there is some censorship, some protection against frightening insights into our repressed experiences and emotions, and that protection takes the form of dream distortion. The “message” our unconscious expresses in our dreams, which is the dream’s underlying meaning, or latent content, is altered so that we don’t readily recognize it through processes called displacement and condensation. Dream displacement occurs whenever we use a “safe” person, event, or object as a “stand-in” to represent a more threatening person, event, or object. For example, I may dream that an elementary school teacher is sexually molesting me in order to express (and at the same time avoid) my unconscious knowledge that one of my parents sexually molested me. Condensation occurs during a dream whenever we use a single dream image or event to represent more than one unconscious wound or conflict. For example, my dream that I’m battling a ferocious bear might represent psychological “battles” or conflicts both at home and at work. Or, to expand on the earlier example, my dream that I am being sexually molested by an elementary school teacher might represent my unconscious feeling that my self-esteem is under attack by any number of family members, friends, and colleagues. (A single dream event may thus be a product of both displacement and condensation.)

由于梦境中会发生位移和凝缩，这些过程统称为初级修正。初级修正掩盖了潜意识信息或梦境的潜在内容后，我们所看到的梦境就是梦境的显性内容。上面描述的梦境意象——小学老师性骚扰我以及我与一头凶猛的熊搏斗——就是显性内容的例子。这些意象的真正含义是梦境的潜在内容，而这需要解读。小学老师是否代表我的父母？性骚扰的意象是否代表对我自尊心的言语攻击？熊是否代表某种心理冲突？如果是，这种冲突是什么？因此，在解读梦境时，我们的目标是回忆起显性内容并尝试揭示潜在内容。然而，我们必须记住，即使在意识层面，我们也极有可能无意识地改变梦境，以进一步保护自己。知道一些令人痛苦的事情。例如，我们可能会忘记梦境的某些部分，或者对这些部分的记忆与实际发生的情况有所不同。这个过程发生在我们清醒的时候，被称为二次修正。

Because displacement and condensation occur while we dream, these processes are referred to collectively as primary revision. What we actually dream, once primary revision has disguised the unconscious message, or the dream’s latent content, is the dream’s manifest content. The dream images described above – images of an elementary school teacher molesting me and of myself battling a ferocious bear – are examples of manifest content. What these images actually mean is the dreams’ latent content, and that is a matter of interpretation. Is the elementary school teacher a stand-in for one of my parents, or are the images of sexual molestation a stand-in for verbal attacks on my self-esteem? Does the bear represent a psychological conflict, and if so, what is that conflict? In interpreting our dreams then, our goal is to recall the manifest content and try to uncover the latent content. However, we must remember that, at this conscious stage as well, we’re very liable to unconsciously change the dream in order to further protect ourselves from knowing what is too painful to know. For example, we might forget certain parts of the dream or remember those parts somewhat differently from how they actually occurred. This process, which takes place when we are awake, is called secondary revision.

或许可以将梦境的显性内容视为一种梦境象征，其解读方式与解读其他任何符号的方式大致相同。但需要注意的是，特定符号与其含义之间并非一一对应。也就是说，虽然某些意象在不同梦者之间往往具有相同的象征意义（至少在同一文化背景下），但我们在梦中呈现无​​意识体验的方式也存在显著的个体差异。因此，为了提高梦境解读的准确性，我们必须随着时间的推移，了解自己在梦中呈现某些想法、感受和人物的倾向，并且必须了解特定梦境意象出现的情境：在特定梦境意象出现之前、期间和之后，梦中发生了什么？

It may be helpful to think of the dream’s manifest content as a kind of dream symbolism that can be interpreted in much the same way we interpret symbols of any kind, if we keep in mind that there is no one-to-one correspondence between a given symbol and its meaning. That is, while there are some images that tend to have the same symbolic meaning from dreamer to dreamer, at least if those dreamers are members of the same culture, there are also important individual differences in the ways we represent our unconscious experience in our dreams. So to increase our chances of interpreting our dreams accurately, we must learn over time how we tend to represent certain ideas, feelings, and people in our dreams, and we must know the context in which a particular dream image occurred: what happened in the dream before, during, and after a particular dream image appeared?

梦境解析通常遵循一些通用原则，具体如下。由于做梦者在梦中创造了所有“人物”，因此从某种意义上说，我们梦见的每个人实际上都是我们自身心理体验的一部分，我们在梦中将其投射到一个替代者身上。例如，如果我梦见我的姐姐生下一个死胎，我可能梦见自己生下了一个死胎（一段失败的感情？一段失败的事业？一次失败的艺术尝试？），或者梦见自己就是一个死胎（我是否感到被抛弃？无助？抑郁？）。正如这个例子所示，关于孩子的梦几乎总是揭示我们对自身或我们内心深处那个可能仍然受到某种伤害的孩子的感受。

Certain general principles of dream interpretation tend to apply in most cases, and they are as follows. Because dreamers create all the “characters” in their dreams, there is a real sense in which each person we dream about is really a part of our own psychological experience that we project during the dream onto a stand-in. If I dream that my sister gives birth to a stillborn child, for example, I might be dreaming either that I have given birth to a stillborn child (a failed relationship? a failed career? a failed artistic endeavor?) or that I am a stillborn child (am I feeling abandoned? helpless? depressed?). As this example makes evident, dreams about children almost always reveal something about our feelings toward ourselves or toward the child that is still within us and that is probably still wounded in some way.

鉴于性取向是我们心理状态的重要反映，我们关于性别角色或我们作为性存在对自身和他人的态度的梦境也具有启示意义。为了解读这些梦境，我们需要注意其中可能出现的男性和女性意象。男性意象，或称阳具象征，可能包括高塔、火箭、枪支、箭矢、刀剑等等。简而言之，如果它是直立的、会爆炸的，或者呈蛇形，它就可能具有阳具象征的功能。例如，如果我梦见用枪指着我的朋友，我可能是在无意识地表达对这位朋友或对其他可以替代这位朋友的人（例如我朋友的伴侣或我的伴侣）的性侵犯。此外，我的性侵犯可以从多个角度解读：重点是性本身，还是侵犯行为，抑或两者兼而有之？我究竟是渴望朋友的伴侣，还是嫉妒朋友的伴侣？我究竟是想在与伴侣的性关系中更加主动，还是想伤害伴侣的性自尊，就像伴侣伤害过我一样？要判断哪种解释正确，需要更多类似案例的数据。梦境、清醒时的行为模式，以及我对梦境和梦中人物的感受的诚实分析，都与此息息相关。类似地，如果我梦见自己被枪指着，这可能表达了一种潜意识里的感受，即我的性取向或身份认同正受到剥削或威胁。

Given that our sexuality is such an important reflection of our psychological being, our dreams about our gender roles or about our attitudes toward ourselves and others as sexual beings are also revealing. In order to interpret these dreams, we need to be aware of the male and female imagery that can occur in them. Male imagery, or phallic symbols, can include towers, rockets, guns, arrows, swords, and the like. In short, if it stands upright, goes off, or has a serpentine form, it might be functioning as a phallic symbol. For example, if I dream that I am holding my friend at gunpoint, I might be expressing unconscious sexual aggression toward that friend or toward someone else for whom that friend is a safe stand-in (such as my friend’s mate or my mate). In addition, my sexual aggression might be interpreted in a number of ways: is the emphasis on the sexual, on the aggression, or on both? Do I desire my friend’s mate, or am I jealous of my friend’s mate? Do I want to become more assertive in my sexual relationship with my mate, or do I want to hurt my mate’s sexual self-image as my mate has hurt mine? To decide which interpretation is correct requires more data in the form of other similar dreams, patterns in my waking behavior, and an honest analysis of my feelings about the dream and about the people involved. Analogously, if I dream that I am being held at gunpoint, I might be expressing an unconscious feeling that my sexuality, or my identity in general, is being exploited or endangered.

女性意象可以包括洞穴、房间、围墙花园（就像我们在描绘圣母玛利亚的画作中看到的那样）、杯子，或者任何类型的围栏和容器。如果某个意象可以代表子宫，那么它就可能具有女性意象的功能。因此，如果我梦见自己被困在一个狭小黑暗的房间里，或者迷失其中，我可能是在表达一种潜意识里的恐惧，害怕母亲控制我，或者害怕自己从未真正成熟为人。也许我同时表达了这两种恐惧，因为这两个问题肯定是相关的。女性意象还可以包括牛奶、水果和其他食物，以及盛放食物的容器，例如瓶子或杯子（是的，这里与子宫意象有重叠之处）——换句话说，任何可以代表乳房的东西，而乳房本身又代表着情感的滋养。所以，如果我梦见自己正试图用一小瓶快用完的牛奶喂一群饥饿的小猫（男女都可能做这种梦），这可能表达了我潜意识里的一种感受：我的孩子、配偶或雇主——或者他们所有人——对我的要求太多，或者我给自己施加了太多照顾他人的压力。类似地，如果我梦见自己饥饿或正在寻找食物，这可能表达了我潜意识里对情感关怀的需求。

Female imagery can include caves, rooms, walled-in gardens (like the ones we see in paintings representing the Virgin Mary), cups, or enclosures and containers of any kind. If the image can be a stand-in for the womb, then it might be functioning as female imagery. Thus, if I dream I am trapped or lost in a small, dark room, I might be expressing an unconscious fear of my mother’s control over me or an unconscious fear that I have never completely matured as a human being. Perhaps I’m expressing both, for these two problems are certainly related. Female imagery can also include milk, fruit, and other kinds of food as well as the containers in which food is delivered, such as bottles or cups (yes, there is an overlap here with womb imagery) – in other words, anything that can be a stand-in for the breast, which is itself a stand-in for emotional nurturing. So if I dream that I am trying to feed a litter of hungry kittens from a small and rapidly diminishing bottle of milk (a dream that either gender can have), I might be expressing an unconscious feeling that too much is being asked of me by my children or by my spouse or by my employer – or by all of them – or that I am putting too much pressure on myself to take care of others. Analogously, if I dream I am hungry or looking for food, I might be expressing an unconscious need for emotional nurturing.

说到其他类型的象征意义，如果我梦见水——水是流动的、变化的，有时令人舒缓，有时又充满危险，而且往往比表面看起来更深邃——那么我很有可能梦见的是我的性欲、情感领域或潜意识领域。所以，梦见自己即将被海啸吞没，可能暗示着我害怕被某种被压抑的情绪所淹没，而这种情绪可能即将爆发。当然，水也与我们在子宫中的经历有关，因此，与水有关的梦，尤其是梦见浸入水中，也可能与我们和母亲的关系有关。梦见建筑物可能代表我与自身的关系，阁楼或地下室可能象征着潜意识。或者，梦见建筑物也可能代表我与某个机构的关系，例如教堂、学校、我工作的公司或法律（法律代表着社会规则和定义，因此可能象征着我的超我）。尽管我们常常梦到自己明知存在的恐惧和创伤——这些显然是我们意识体验的一部分——但梦到这些担忧可能表明我们需要进一步处理它们，它们以我们尚未准备好承认的方式折磨着我们。当然，反复出现的梦境或梦境意象是我们潜意识担忧最可靠的指标。

To move to other kinds of symbols, if I dream about water – which is fluid, changeable, sometimes soothing, sometimes dangerous, and often deeper than it looks – chances are good that I’m dreaming about my sexuality or the realm of the emotions or the realm of the unconscious. So a dream that I’m about to be overwhelmed by a tidal wave probably indicates some fear of being overwhelmed by a repressed emotion that I fear is about to erupt. Of course, water is also related to our experience in the womb, so dreams that involve water, especially immersion in water, might also be about our relationships with our mothers. Dreams about buildings may refer to my relationship with myself, with the attic or the basement as the stand-in for the unconscious. Or dreams about buildings may refer to my relationship with some institution that the building represents for me, for example, the church, the school, the company for which I work, or the law (which, because it represents social rules and definitions, might be a stand-in for my superego). Although we might often dream about fears and wounds that we know we have – that are clearly part of our conscious experience – our dreams about these concerns probably indicate that we need to work further on them, that they bite into us in ways we aren’t ready to admit. Of course, recurring dreams or recurring dream images are the most reliable indicators of our unconscious concerns.

无论我们的梦境多么可怕或令人不安，它们都是相对安全的宣泄渠道，可以释放潜意识中的创伤、恐惧、罪恶的欲望和未解决的冲突。因为正如我们所见，它们以伪装的形式出现，而我们只能在准备好的范围内解读它们。此外，如果梦境变得过于可怕，我们会醒来，就像噩梦中我们通常会醒来一样。然而，如果我的噩梦开始在我清醒时出现——也就是说，如果我的防御机制崩溃并非暂时性的，如果我的焦虑无法缓解，如果被压抑的真相以一种我既无法掩饰也无法应对的方式呈现在我的意识面前——那么我就处于危机或创伤之中。

Regardless of how frightening or disturbing our dreams are, they are relatively safe outlets for unconscious wounds, fears, guilty desires, and unresolved conflicts because, as we have seen, they come to us in disguised form, and we will interpret them only to whatever extent we are ready to do so. In addition, if a dream becomes too threatening, we will wake up, as we most often do during nightmares. However, if my nightmares begin to occur while I’m awake – that is, if the breakdown of my defenses is more than temporary, if my anxiety cannot be abated, if the truth hidden by repression comes out before my conscious self in a manner I can neither disguise nor handle – then I am in crisis, or trauma.

死亡的意义

The meaning of death

危机将我一直未能处理、亟需解决的伤痛、恐惧、愧疚的欲望或未解决的冲突暴露出来。过去如潮水般涌来，因为我终于看清了真相。这就是我通过危机认识自我的方式。当然， “创伤”一词也用来指代那些会在我们心理上留下伤痕的痛苦经历。因此，我可能会经历童年时期因疾病、意外或自杀而失去兄弟姐妹的创伤，并在成年后经历创伤或危机，即被我压抑的关于那场死亡的所有愧疚、否认和冲突所淹没。我也可能看到，例如，我的父母是如何在无意识中加剧我的愧疚感，以减轻他们自己的愧疚。

Crisis brings into the spotlight wounds, fears, guilty desires, or unresolved conflicts that I have failed to deal with and that demand action. I am flooded by the past because I can now see what was really going on. This is how I can know myself through crisis. The word trauma is also used, of course, to refer to a painful experience that scars us psychologically. Thus, I might experience the childhood trauma of losing a sibling to illness, accidental death, or suicide and, in later life, experience the trauma, or crisis, of being flooded by all the guilt, denial, and conflict I’ve repressed concerning that death. And I might also see, for example, the ways in which my parents unconsciously encouraged my guilt in order to relieve their own.

事实上，我们与死亡的关系，无论童年时期是否遭受过死亡创伤，都是我们心理体验的主要组织者。在探讨我们与死亡的关系如何以这种方式运作之前，有必要指出，在我看来，死亡似乎是精神分析理论家们最为头疼的主题，这或许是因为死亡在他们自身以及所有人的心理体验中都占据着举足轻重的地位。人们往往倾向于将死亡视为一种抽象概念——也就是说，他们以一种让我们无法切身感受到死亡力量的方式来探讨死亡——大概是因为死亡的力量太过令人恐惧。因此，即便理论家们直接探讨死亡这一主题，或者说尤其当他们这样做的时候，他们有时也会以一种刻意与死亡保持情感距离的方式来探讨死亡，从而也与我们保持距离。我认为这就是——仅举一例——许多精神分析理论家仍然坚持的理论背后的原因，即人类有一种“内在的”死亡驱动力，一种与生俱来的遗忘冲动，通常被称为死亡驱动力或死亡本能。

In fact, our relationship to death, whether or not we are traumatized by it in childhood, is a principal organizer of our psychological experience. Before we examine how our relationship to death operates in this way, it is important to note that death is the subject that, it seems to me, has given psychoanalytic theorists the most trouble, probably because of its importance in their own, as well as everyone else’s, psychological experience. There has been some tendency to treat death as an abstraction – that is, to theorize about it in ways that don’t allow us to feel its force too intimately – presumably because its force is too frightening. So even when, or especially when, theorists have addressed the subject of death directly, they sometimes have done so in ways that tend to keep it at an emotional distance from themselves and, therefore, from us. I think this is the reason – to cite just one example – behind the theory, still held by many psychoanalytic theorists, that human beings have a “built-in” drive toward death, an inborn compulsion toward oblivion, commonly called the death drive, or thanatos.

认为人类具有死亡本能，是为了解释我们所看到的令人震惊的自毁行为：既包括那些似乎执意在心理上（即便不是生理上）自我毁灭的个体，也包括那些连年战乱和内讧不断的国家，这些国家往往如同集体自杀一般。因此，我们这个物种的构成中必然存在某种东西，可以解释这种死亡行为，这种心理和生理上的自我毁灭。当然，当我们把这种死亡行为概念化为一种本能，一种我们所有人共有且无法避免的本能时，我们就无需深入探究其运作机制了。试图改变它；毕竟，我们所做的一切都无法改变人类与生俱来的本能。这就是为什么我称死亡本能的概念为抽象概念，一种只存在于概念层面、与具体经验世界毫无关联的观念。虽然死亡本身当然是具体的现实，但死亡本能的概念，正如抽象概念一样，将我们的思想和情感从日常的行动和责任世界中抽离出来。而这正是我认为某些理论家对死亡的抽象解释如此感兴趣的原因。这类解释将我们从日常世界中抽离出来，而我们正是在这个世界里进行着心理和生理上的自我毁灭行为。

In suggesting that human beings have a death drive, the attempt is to account for the alarming degree of self-destructive behavior we see both in individuals, who seem bent on destroying themselves psychologically if not physically, and in whole nations, whose constant wars and internal conflicts often seem much like a form of mass suicide. There must be something, then, in our makeup as a species to explain this death work, this psychological and physical self-destruction. Of course, when we conceptualize our death work as a drive, as something common to all of us and unavoidable, we are off the hook of having to probe too deeply into its workings or to try to change it; after all, nothing we do can alter an inborn human drive. This is why I call the concept of the death drive an abstraction, an idea that operates only on the conceptual level, with no connection to the concrete world of experience. Although death itself is, of course, a concrete reality, the concept of the death drive takes our thoughts and our feelings out of the everyday world of action and responsibility, just as abstractions do. And this is exactly why I think some theorists have found abstract explanations of death attractive. Such explanations take us out of the everyday world in which our acts of psychological and physical self-destruction occur.

理解我们与死亡关系的一种更有效、也更准确的方式，是将其置于我们其他心理体验的语境中进行考察，因为死亡是我们心理体验不可分割的一部分。如果我们这样做，就会发现死亡，尤其是对死亡的恐惧，与许多其他心理现实密切相关。我们还会发现，由于个体心理构成的差异，他们对死亡的反应也各不相同。换句话说，虽然我即将描述的这些过程可能发生在我们所有人身上，但它们在每个个体身上发生的程度和结果都会有所不同。

A more useful, and I think more accurate, way of understanding our relationship to death is to examine it in relation to the rest of our psychological experience, of which it is an integral part. If we do this, we will see that death, in particular fear of death, is intimately connected to a number of other psychological realities. And we will see that individuals respond to death in various ways because of differences in their psychological makeup. In other words, while the processes I am about to describe probably occur in all of us, they will occur to different degrees and with different results in each individual.

首先，对我们许多人来说，想到死亡，首先想到的就是被抛弃的恐惧，害怕孤独。死亡是终极的抛弃：无论我们与亲人多么亲近，无论我们在社会中多么重要，当我们死去时，我们都将孤独地死去。即使我们与两百多人一起死于空难，我们每个人的死亡也是各自独立的。因此，宗教信仰所能提供的最大慰藉之一，就是向我们保证，我们不会孤独地死去，死后也不会孤独：上帝会与我们同在，陪伴着我们。即使我们认识的所有人都抛弃了我们，他也不会抛弃我们。

First and foremost, for many of us, the thought of our own death keys into our fear of abandonment, our fear of being alone. Death is the ultimate abandonment: no matter how close we are to our loved ones, no matter how important we are in our communities, when we die we die alone. Even if we die in a plane crash with two hundred other people, we each die our own private death. Thus, one of the greatest comforts religious belief can offer is to assure us that we will not die alone and that after we die we will not be alone: God will be there for us and with us. He will not abandon us even when everyone else we know has done so.

当我们恐惧他人的死亡时，被抛弃的恐惧也扮演着重要角色。当孩子失去父母，当成年人失去配偶时，那种难以承受的失落感往往是一种被抛弃的感觉。你怎么能离开我？你不爱我了吗？我做错了什么？有时，丧亲者甚至会感到被上帝抛弃。在这种情况下，无论我们是否意识到，亲人的离世都会触动我们内心的愧疚：我一定是哪里做得不够好；我一定是做错了什么，否则我不会受到这样的惩罚。事实上，对这种失去的恐惧，对这种强烈心理痛苦的恐惧，或许是我们当中有些人不敢与他人走得太近，不敢爱得太深的最大原因。如果我能有所保留，不将自己完全交付给所爱之人，那么当所爱之人离世时，我就能更好地承受失去的痛苦。

Fear of abandonment also plays a role when we fear the death of others. When children lose a parent, when adults lose a spouse, the overwhelming feeling of loss is often a feeling of abandonment. How could you leave me? Don’t you love me? What did I do wrong? Sometimes the bereaved feel abandoned even by God. In this context, whether we realize it or not, the death of a loved one pushes our guilt buttons: somehow I must have been inadequate; I must have done something wrong or I wouldn’t be punished in this way. In fact, fear of such a loss, of such intense psychological pain, is probably the biggest reason why some of us are afraid to get too close to another person or are afraid to love too deeply. If I can hold something back, not give my whole self over to the loved one, then I will be better able to bear the loss when the beloved dies.

因此，对死亡的恐惧——以及我们之前看到的其他原因——常常导致人们对亲密关系的恐惧。这解释了为什么对死亡的恐惧常常会演变成对生命的恐惧。也就是说，我们对死亡、对失去生命的恐惧，会导致我们害怕与生命建立亲密关系。“当你一无所有时，你就没有什么可失去的了”，正如许多蓝调和民谣所唱的那样。这种对生命的恐惧这种恐惧也可以表现为对风险的恐惧。我最害怕的，也是最终的损失，就是死亡。因此，我不能冒任何可能导致死亡的风险。但生命本身最终也是不可避免的结局是死亡。因此，我不能冒险去活下去。我必须尽可能地让自己远离死亡，尽可能地减少行动，尽可能地减少感受：我要努力让自己在情感上麻木，以避免被死亡所伤害。如果这种对死亡的态度走向极端，最终会导致自杀。我对失去生命的强烈恐惧，使得活着如此痛苦和可怕，以至于死亡成了我唯一的解脱。

Fear of death is thus often responsible – along with other reasons, as we saw earlier – for fear of intimacy. This is one of the ways we can see how fear of death often results in fear of life. That is, our fear of death, of losing our life, can result in our fear of being intimately attached to life. “When you ain’t got nothin’, you got nothin’ to lose,” as so many blues and folk songs have pointed out. This fear of life can also be played out as a fear of risk. The ultimate loss, of which I am utterly terrified, is death. Therefore, I can’t take any risk that might result in death. But life itself ultimately and inevitably results in death. Therefore, I can’t risk living my life. I must somehow remove myself from it by doing as little as possible and by feeling as little as possible: I will try to be emotionally dead to avoid being hurt by death. Taken to its logical extreme, this relationship to death will result in suicide. My intense fear of losing my life makes living so painful and frightening that my only escape is death.

如果我们更深入地思考，意识到我们对死亡的恐惧并非仅仅是对生理死亡的恐惧，而是对我们大多数人而言，转化为对各种失去的恐惧——失去伴侣的关注、失去孩子的爱、失去健康、失去工作、失去容貌、失去金钱——那么我们就能理解，为什么死亡，即便不是生理死亡，至少在潜意识层面，如此具有吸引力：如果我感觉不到任何东西，我就不会受到伤害。如果我们意识到，我们最初的死亡体验并非生理上的，而是我们大多数人在第一次感受到被父母抛弃时所经历的心理上的“死亡”，那么我们就能理解，我们早期的被抛弃经历是如何塑造了我们对死亡的恐惧。这种不愿感受的渴望，这种为了逃避痛苦而将自己与生活隔绝的渴望，或许是最常见的“死亡工作”。

If we complicate matters by realizing that our fear of death is not merely fear of biological death but translates for most of us into fear of loss in general – loss of my mate’s attention, loss of my children’s love, loss of my health, loss of my job, loss of my looks, loss of my money – then we can see how death, emotional death if not biological death, is so attractive, at least on the unconscious level: if I don’t feel anything, then I can’t be hurt. And if we realize that our first experience of death is not biological at all, but the psychological “death” most of us suffered the first time we felt abandoned by a parent, then we can see the ways in which our early experiences of abandonment created our fear of death. This desire not to feel, this desire to insulate ourselves from life in order to insulate ourselves from pain, is probably the most common form of death work.

鉴于死亡在我们生活中扮演着如此重要的角色，我们对它着迷也就不足为奇了。事实上，我认为可以合理地得出结论：我们越恐惧，就越着迷。换句话说，死亡在我们心理层面上扮演的角色越重要，我们就越会被各种形式的死亡所吸引，即便它伴随着恐惧：我们永远不会看太多关于自然灾害的暴力电影或纪录片；我们总是忍不住去看路边的车祸现场；我们永远不会看太多关于虐童、强奸和艾滋病的新闻报道；我们永远不会看太多关于杀害配偶或情人配偶的电视电影，也不会看太多那些功能失调关系中的成员毫无自知之明地展示他们功能失调的脱口秀节目，就像孩子展示他们最喜欢的玩具一样。我们对媒体呈现的死亡和死亡工作的着迷，正是我们如何将自身的恐惧和问题投射到自身之外的人和事上的又一个例证。因此，这种迷恋起到了一种防御作用：如果我想到城另一边的虐童者（或者与我来自不同社会阶层或种族背景的人），我就会将注意力从我遭受虐待的方式或我对他人的虐待方式上转移开来。

Is it any wonder then, given the enormous role that death plays in our lives, that we should be fascinated with it? In fact, I think it’s reasonable to conclude that the greater our fear is, the greater our fascination becomes. Put another way, the greater the role that death work plays in our psychological being, the greater our attraction is, despite the horror that accompanies it, to death in all its forms: we can’t see too many violent movies or docudramas about natural disasters; we can’t keep our eyes off the roadside car wreck; we can’t see too many news reports about child abuse, rape, and AIDS; we can’t see too many made-for-television movies about people who kill their spouses or their lovers’ spouses, or too many talk shows on which members of dysfunctional relationships display their dysfunctions apparently with no more self-awareness than children displaying their favorite toys. Our fascination with media representations of death and death work is another example of how we project our fears and problems onto people and events outside ourselves. This fascination thus operates as a defense: if I think about the child abuser on the other side of town (or from a different social class or ethnic background from mine) I divert my attention from the ways in which I’ve been abused or from my abuse of others.

性的意义

The meaning of sexuality

另一个往往需要用抽象解释来解释的心理体验领域——正如我们前面看到的，这表明它在我们生活中具有可怕的力量——是人类性欲。对一些科学思想家来说，尤其是在过去，性欲是一种生物压力，通过性交行为释放出来。然而，弗洛伊德认为性欲是一种与生俱来的生命肯定驱动力，即爱欲（eros），并将其与死亡驱动力（thanatos）相对立。他的研究远不止于此。首先，弗洛伊德意识到，我们的性欲是我们身份认同不可分割的一部分，因此与我们感受愉悦的能力密切相关，而这种愉悦感通常不被认为是性方面的。这就是为什么他认为，即使是婴儿也是性存在，他们会经历口唇期、肛门期和生殖器期——在这些阶段中，愉悦感会集中在身体的不同部位。（你可以想象这在维多利亚时代的社会引起了怎样的轩然大波和误解！）理论家们不断拓展弗洛伊德的洞见，如今的精神分析学认为，我们的性欲与身份认同之间存在着密切的联系，因为我们性存在的起源在于童年时期自我意识的肯定或瓦解。因此，性欲是我们整体心理状态最清晰、最稳定的晴雨表之一。对精神分析而言，性欲是人类无法回避的现实，我们必须与之建立关系。性欲并非生物本能的驱力释放机制，而是意义的体现。因此，在分析性行为时，恰当的精神分析问题是：“我在性行为中表达或实践了哪些有意识和无意识的意义和目的？”我是否利用性来“换取”伴侣想要的东西？我是否通过拒绝性行为来惩罚伴侣？我是否完全回避性行为？我是否寻求与不同的人频繁发生性关系？值得注意的是，后两个问题都暗示着对亲密关系的恐惧——如果我与某人走得太近，我会迷失自我或受到情感伤害——因为频繁更换性伴侣可以像完全回避性行为一样有效地保护我们，避免与任何一个人走得太近。

Another area of psychological experience that has tended to elicit abstract explanations – and as we saw above, this points to its frightening power in our lives – is human sexuality. For some scientific thinkers, especially in the past, sexuality was a matter of a biological pressure that is discharged in the act of sexual intercourse. Freud, however, considered sexual desire an inborn life-affirming drive, or eros, and placed it in opposition to the death drive, or thanatos. And he didn’t stop there. For one thing, Freud realized that our sexuality is part and parcel of our identity and thus relates to our capacity to feel pleasure in ways that are not generally considered sexual. This is why he believed that even infants are sexual beings who pass through stages – oral, anal, and genital – in which pleasure is focused in different parts of the body. (You can imagine the furor and the misunderstanding that caused in Victorian society!) Theorists have continued to build on Freud’s insights, and psychoanalysis today sees a close connection between our sexuality and our identity because the origin of our sexual being is in the nature of the affirmation or disruption of our sense of self that occurs in childhood. Therefore, our sexuality is one of the clearest and most consistent barometers of our psychological state in general. For psychoanalysis, our sexuality is an inescapable human reality to which we must live a relationship. Our sexuality is not a matter of biological drivedischarge mechanisms but a matter of meanings. In analyzing sexual behavior then, the appropriate psychoanalytic question is “What conscious and unconscious meanings and purposes do I express or enact in my sexuality?” Do I use sex to “purchase” something I want from my mate? Do I withhold sex to punish my mate? Do I avoid sexual encounters altogether? Do I seek frequent sexual encounters with different people? It is interesting to note that these last two questions both suggest a fear of intimacy – if I get too close to someone I will lose myself or be emotionally harmed – because varying our sexual partners can protect us from getting close to any one person as effectively as avoiding sexual encounters completely.

当然，性行为也是我们文化的产物，因为我们的文化制定了恰当的性行为规范，以及正常和异常性行为的定义。（对于精神分析而言，正常和异常之间并没有本质区别，问题不在于道德与不道德的行为，而仅仅在于个体之间的心理差异，问题在于非破坏性行为与破坏性行为。）社会关于性的规则和定义构成了我们超我的重要组成部分，也就是我们（有意识或无意识地）内化并体验为是非观的社会价值观和禁忌。虽然“良心”一词通常意味着一些好事——正如迪士尼的吉米尼蟋蟀所说，“让你的良心指引你”——但“超我”一词却常常意味着在不应该感到内疚的时候感到内疚，这种内疚感仅仅是因为我们受到社会（通常是通过家庭）的影响而产生的，例如，即使我们知道一份薪水较低的工作更有成就感或社会意义，我们仍然会因为接受这份工作而感到内疚；或者，像我们中的许多人一样，在婚前与心爱的人发生性关系而感到内疚。

Of course, sexual behavior is also a product of our culture because our culture sets down the rules of proper sexual conduct and the definitions of normal and abnormal sexual behavior. (For psychoanalysis, there is no meaningful difference between normal and abnormal, and the issue isn’t one of moral versus immoral behavior; there are merely psychological differences among individuals, and the issue is one of nondestructive versus destructive behavior.) Society’s rules and definitions concerning sexuality form a large part of our superego, or the social values and taboos that we internalize (consciously or unconsciously) and experience as our sense of right and wrong. Whereas the word conscience, as it is usually used, generally implies something good – as Disney’s Jiminy Cricket says, “Let your conscience be your guide” – the word superego often implies feeling guilty when we shouldn’t, feeling guilty only because we are socially programmed (usually through the family) to feel so, as when we feel guilty for taking a lower-paying job even when we know that it is a more satisfying or socially important one, or when we feel guilty, as many of us still do, for having sexual relations with our beloved prior to marriage.

超我与本我（我们被压抑的攻击性欲望的心理储存库）以及力比多（性欲）直接对立。本我一心只想满足各种被禁止的欲望——权力欲、性欲、娱乐欲、食物欲——而不考虑后果。换句话说，本我主要由自我压抑的、因社会习俗所禁止的欲望构成。因此，超我——或者说文化禁忌的内化——决定了本我将包含哪些欲望。自我——通过感官体验外部世界的意识自我，也是我们自我形象和稳定感的来源——试图在超我和本我之间扮演裁判的角色，这三者都由彼此之间的关系所定义：它们彼此之间并非独立运作，其中之一的变化总是会牵涉到其他两者的变化。因此，在很大程度上，自我是社会禁止我们拥有的东西与我们（因此）想要的东西之间冲突的产物。因此，自我、本我和超我之间的关系，既反映了我们的文化，也反映了我们自身。

The superego is in direct opposition to the id, the psychological reservoir of our repressed aggressive desires, and to our libido, or sexual energy. The id is devoted solely to the gratification of prohibited desires of all kinds – desire for power, for sex, for amusement, for food – without an eye to consequences. In other words, the id consists largely of those desires repressed by the ego because they are forbidden by social convention. Thus, the superego – or the internalization of cultural taboos – determines which desires the id will contain. The ego – the conscious self that experiences the external world through the senses and is the source of our self-image and feeling of stability – tries to play referee between the id and superego, and all three are defined by their relationships to one another: none acts independently of the others and a change in one always involves changes in the other two. In this way, the ego is, to a large degree, the product of conflicts between what society says we can’t have and what we (therefore) want. For this reason, the relationships among ego, id, and superego tell us as much about our culture as they do about ourselves.

事实上，正是对弗洛伊德所处文化背景的理解，帮助我们更深刻地理解了他早期一些看似与我们自身世界观相悖的概念。例如，许多女性，无论她们是否自认为是女权主义者，都难以相信小女孩在意识到小男孩有阴茎后会感到“阴茎嫉妒”（即渴望拥有阴茎），或者小男孩在意识到小女孩没有阴茎后会感到“阉割焦虑”（即害怕失去阴茎）。然而，当我们意识到弗洛伊德观察这些现象的文化背景时，这两个现象的解释就变得清晰明了：维多利亚时代社会对性别角色的僵化定义，被用来压迫各个年龄段的女性，并将男性提升到人类活动各个领域的主导地位。当一个小女孩意识到小男孩拥有她本不该渴望​​的权利和特权时，她（至少在潜意识里）想要成为小男孩也就不足为奇了。换句话说，当你看到“阴茎嫉妒”时，其实是在说“权力嫉妒”。小女孩嫉妒的是权力以及与之相关的一切——自尊、乐趣、自由、免受异性身体侵犯的表面上的安全感。而哪个小男孩在意识到自己比小女孩更优越、更有权力时，不会担心失去这种优势呢？“你是个女孩，你这个娘娘腔！”这句话能够伤害小男孩（甚至大男孩！），因为它让他们面临失去权力的威胁。因此，阉割焦虑或许最好理解为害怕被降级到女性所处的无权地位。

Indeed, it is an appreciation of the cultural context within which Freud worked that has helped us come to a more meaningful understanding of some of Freud’s early concepts that seem to contradict our own sense of how the world works. For example, many women, whether they consider themselves feminists or not, have a difficult time believing that little girls, upon realizing that little boys have penises, suffer from penis envy, or the desire to have a penis, or that little boys, upon realizing that little girls don’t have penises, suffer from castration anxiety, or the fear that they will lose their penises. The explanation for these two phenomena becomes clear, however, when we realize the cultural context within which Freud observed them: Victorian society’s rigid definition of gender roles, which was used to oppress females of all ages and to elevate males to positions of dominance in all spheres of human activity. Is it any wonder that a little girl will want (at least unconsciously) to be a little boy when she realizes that little boys have rights and privileges she isn’t supposed to even desire? In other words, when you see “penis envy” read “power envy.” It’s power and all that seems to go with it – self-esteem, fun, freedom, apparent safety from physical violation by the opposite sex – that little girls envy. And what little boy, upon realizing his social superiority to, and power over, little girls, isn’t going to have some anxiety about losing it? “You’re a girl, you sissy!” has the power to wound little boys (and big boys!) because it threatens them with just such a loss of power. Castration anxiety is thus perhaps best understood as fear of demotion to the powerless position occupied by females.

拉康精神分析

Lacanian psychoanalysis

虽然我们在本章迄今为止讨论的经典精神分析理论长期以来一直是文学研究的标准精神分析方法，但还有一种……一种非传统的精神分析理论正逐渐进入本科英语课程：法国精神分析学家雅克·拉康（1901-1981）的理论。拉康的作品相当抽象，常常含糊不清，几乎总是难以理解。事实上，他认为，关于无意识的论述应该含糊不清、难以理解，因为无意识本身就是含糊的（例如，它在我们的梦境、行为和艺术创作中的体现通常具有多种含义），而且无意识本身就难以理解。此外，拉康的许多论述的真正含义在诠释者之间存在着相当大的分歧。最后，拉康有时会随着时间的推移改变一些关键术语的含义。尽管存在这些挑战，我认为我们至少需要对拉康精神分析的一些主要概念进行初步了解，因为这些概念开始出现在学生的写作中，而且常常被错误使用。

While the classical psychoanalytic theory we’ve discussed so far in this chapter has long been the standard psychoanalytic approach to literature, there is a brand of nontraditional psychoanalytic theory that is beginning to make its way into the undergraduate English curriculum: that of French psychoanalyst Jacques Lacan (1901–81). Lacan’s work is rather abstract, often ambiguous, and almost always difficult to understand. In fact, he claimed that writing about the unconscious should be ambiguous and difficult to understand because the unconscious is itself ambiguous (its manifestations in our dreams, our behavior, and our artistic production, for example, usually have multiple meanings), and the unconscious is difficult to understand. Furthermore, there is a good deal of disagreement among interpreters of Lacan concerning what he actually intended by many of his statements. Finally, Lacan sometimes changed the meanings of some of his key terms over time. Despite these challenges, however, I think we need at least to take an introductory look at some of the main concepts of Lacanian psychoanalysis because these concepts are beginning to show up in students’ writing, and all too often they are being used incorrectly.

例如，你很快就会看到，“象征性”一词在拉康的语境下与我们在文学研究中通常使用该术语时的含义并不相同。然而，理论初学者常常错误地理解拉康对这个术语的用法，仿佛他想表达的是我们通常用来描述文学作品中象征意义的含义，而这种用法与拉康的本意相去甚远。我认为，造成这种问题的原因之一或许在于学生们经常参考的一些拉康精神分析概要，这些概要往往过于简略，几乎和拉康的著作一样抽象。当然，读完本文提供的拉康精神分析概要，你不会立刻对拉康的著作有深刻透彻的理解，但我希望你能更好地理解拉康思想的含义，以及他思想的真正意义。

As you’ll see shortly, for example, the word symbolic doesn’t have the same meaning when Lacan uses it that it has when we generally use the term in our literary studies. Yet beginning students of theory often refer to Lacan’s use of this term as if he intended it to mean what we commonly mean when we write about the symbols in a literary work, a usage of the word that could hardly be farther from Lacan’s. I think perhaps one reason for this problem can be traced to some of the summaries of Lacanian psychoanalysis from which students frequently take their information, which are often too brief and almost as abstract as Lacan’s own writing. Certainly, you won’t emerge from reading the summary of Lacanian psychoanalysis offered here with a profound and thorough understanding of Lacan’s work, but I hope you will have a better sense of what Lacan’s ideas do not mean as well as a clearer grasp of what they do.

为了理解与文学阐释最为相关的拉康概念，我们需要从拉康关于婴儿心理发展的理论入手。拉康认为，在婴儿出生后的最初几个月里，他们将自身和周围环境都体验为随机的、碎片化的、无形的整体。事实上，婴儿甚至无法区分自身与环境，也不知道自身身体的各个部分实际上是自身的一部分，因为他们缺乏能够进行这种理解的自我意识。例如，他们的脚趾就像拨浪鼓或其他环境中的物体一样，只是用来探索、放入口中等等。然而，在6到18个月之间，拉康所说的“镜像阶段”到来了。无论婴儿是在真正的镜子中看到自己，还是在母亲的反应中看到自己的“镜像”，关键在于，婴儿在这个阶段开始发展出一种整体的自我意识，而非无形碎片化的整体意识。换句话说，孩子会逐渐形成一种整体的自我意识，就好像他认同了镜子中映照出的自己的整体形象一样。

In order to understand the Lacanian concepts that are most relevant to literary interpretation, we need to begin at the beginning with Lacan’s theory of the psychological development of the infant. In its early months, Lacan maintains, the infant experiences both itself and its environment as a random, fragmented, formless mass. Indeed, the infant doesn’t even differentiate itself from its environment and doesn’t know that parts of its own body are, in fact, parts of its own body because it doesn’t have a sense of itself that is capable of such an understanding. For example, its own toes are objects to be explored, placed in the mouth, and so forth, just like its rattle or other objects in its environment. Between six and 18 months, however, what Lacan calls the Mirror Stage occurs. Whether the child sees itself in an actual mirror or sees itself “mirrored” back to itself in the reactions of its mother, the point is that the infant now develops during this stage a sense of itself as a whole rather than a formless and fragmented mass. In other words, the child develops a sense of itself as a whole as if it had identified with the whole image of itself that can be seen reflected in a mirror.

当然，孩子无法用语言表达这些感受，因为他们还处于语言发展前的阶段。事实上，拉康认为镜像阶段开启了他所谓的“想象秩序”，也就是意象的世界。这并非想象的世界，而是感知的世界。孩子是通过意象而非语言来体验这个世界的。这是一个充满圆满、完整和喜悦的世界，因为孩子对自身整体的感知带来了一种对环境的掌控幻觉，他们仍然将自身视为环境不可分割的一部分；他们也对母亲拥有掌控感，他们感到与母亲处于一种相互满足的结合状态：我的母亲是我的一切，我也是母亲的一切。请记住，孩子在语言发展前的这种与母亲完全结合，从而完全掌控世界的感受是幻觉，但它仍然非常令人满足，也非常强大。拉康将这种体验称为“母性欲望”，意在暗示前文所述的双向欲望，即母亲对孩子的欲望和孩子对母亲的欲望。在此期间，孩子与母亲的联结感，无论好坏，都是其最初也是最重要的体验。这种最初的二元关系，或称“二元组”，一直持续到孩子习得语言为止——在拉康看来，语言的习得至关重要。

Of course, the child doesn’t have words for these feelings, for it is still preverbal. Indeed, Lacan claims that the Mirror Stage initiates what he calls the Imaginary Order, by which he means the world of images. This is not the world of the imagination, but a world of perception. It’s the world that the child experiences through images rather than through words. And it is a world of fullness, completeness, and delight because with the child’s sense of itself as a whole comes the illusion of control over its environment, of which it still perceives itself as an inseparable part, and over its mother, with whom it feels it is in a union of mutual satisfaction: my mother is all I need and I am all my mother needs. Remember, the child’s preverbal feeling of complete union with its mother and, therefore, complete control over its world is illusory, but it is nonetheless very satisfying and very powerful. Lacan refers to this experience as the Desire of the Mother, intending to imply the two-way desire just described, that is, the desire of the mother for the child and the child’s desire of the mother. During this period, the child’s feeling of connection with its mother is, for good or ill, its first and most important experience, and this primary dyad, or twosome, continues until the child acquires language, a change that, for Lacan, is of paramount importance.

对拉康而言，儿童习得语言具有诸多重要意义。他将儿童习得语言称为其进入象征秩序的开端，因为语言首先是一个符号系统，即一个意义建构的符号系统。我们最初建构的意义——或者更准确地说，是别人为我们建构的意义——包括“我是一个独立的个体”（“我”指的是“我”，而非“你”）以及“我拥有性别”（我是女孩，而非男孩，反之亦然）。因此，我们进入象征秩序必然伴随着与他人分离的体验，而最大的分离便是与我们在想象秩序中与母亲建立的亲密联结的分离。在拉康看来，这种分离构成了我们最重要的丧失体验，并将伴随我们一生。我们将不断寻求各种替代品，无论大小，以弥补与母亲失去的那份联结。我们将终其一生在象征秩序中无意识地追求它——也许找到完美伴侣、获得更多财富、皈依其他宗教、变得更英俊、更受欢迎，或者买辆更炫酷的车、更大的房子，或者任何象征秩序告诉我应该想要的东西，就能重新获得那种合一的感觉——但我们永远无法持续获得完全的满足感。为什么？拉康解释说，这是因为我们所追求的那种满足感，尽管我们并未意识到自己正在追求，却是那种完整、充盈以及与母体/世界合一的感觉，而这种感觉在我们进入象征秩序，也就是我们习得语言之后，就从意识体验中消失了。

For Lacan, the child’s acquisition of language means a number of important things. He refers to the child’s acquisition of language as its initiation into the Symbolic Order, for language is first and foremost a symbolic system of signification, that is, a symbolic system of meaning-making. Among the first meanings we make – or more correctly, that are made for us – are that I am a separate being (“I” am “me,” not “you”) and that I have a gender (I am a girl, not a boy, or vice versa). Our entrance into the Symbolic Order thus involves the experience of separation from others, and the biggest separation is the separation from the intimate union we experienced with our mother during our immersion in the Imaginary Order. For Lacan, this separation constitutes our most important experience of loss, and it is one that will haunt us all our lives. We will seek substitutes great and small for that lost union with our mother. We will spend our lives unconsciously pursuing it in the Symbolic Order – maybe I’ll recapture that feeling of union if I find the perfect mate; if I acquire more money; if I convert to a different religion; if I become better looking; if I become more popular; or if I buy a flashier car, a bigger house, or whatever the Symbolic Order tells me I should want – but we will never be able to sustain a feeling of complete fulfillment. Why? Lacan explains that it’s because the kind of fulfillment we seek, though we don’t realize that we’re seeking it, is that feeling of completeness, plenitude, and union with our mother/our world that disappeared from conscious experience when we entered the Symbolic Order, that is, when we acquired language.

拉康将这种失去的欲望对象称为“objet petit a”，或“小a对象”，其中字母a代表法语单词autre ，意为“其他”。拉康学者对拉康使用这种特殊的程式化简写提出了各种解释。其中之一一个有用的解释可能是，象征秩序将我们从与母亲理想化的结合的语言前世界中分离出来，并将我们的母亲变成了“他者”（与我分离的人），正如它将我们语言前结合世界中的一切也变成了与我们自身分离的人和物的世界一样。为什么拉康用小写的“a”（autre：他者）而不是大写的“Other”（我们稍后会讨论）来指代象征秩序的某种特定属性呢？或许是因为我们与“小他者”（ objet petit a，即我们失去的欲望对象）的关系是如此个人化、如此独特、如此完全私密，而我们在象征秩序中的体验却并非如此。“小他者”只属于我，只影响我。正如我们将看到的，“Other”（大写）则相反，它影响着所有人。

Lacan refers to this lost object of desire as objet petit a, or “object small a,” with the letter a standing for autre, the French word for other. Lacan scholars offer various reasons for Lacan’s use of this particular piece of formulaic shorthand. One useful explanation might be that, in separating us from our preverbal world of idealized union with our mother, the Symbolic Order changed our mother into an other (someone separate from me) just as it changed everything else in our preverbal world of union into a world of people and things separate from ourselves. Why a small a (autre: other) instead of the capitalized Other Lacan uses, as we’ll discuss shortly, to refer to a particular quality of the Symbolic Order? Perhaps it’s because our relationship to our objet petit a, to our lost object of desire, feels so personal, so individual, so utterly private, whereas our experiences in the Symbolic Order do not. Objet petit a is the “little other” that belongs only to me, that influences only me. As we’ll see, Other with a capital O, in contrast, influences everyone.

值得注意的是，“小物件”（objet petit a）也指任何能唤起我对失去之物的压抑渴望的事物。例如，在马塞尔·普鲁斯特的《追忆似水年华》（1913）中，当叙述者自童年以来第一次品尝到一种名为玛德琳的小蛋糕时，他体验到了一种愉悦的回归，仿佛回到了童年时代。他被意想不到的、生动的记忆所淹没。对他而言，玛德琳蛋糕就是“小物件”。对于《了不起的盖茨比》中的杰伊·盖茨比来说，黛西家码头尽头的绿灯或许也是“小物件”，因为有人可能会认为，这盏灯对盖茨比而言，不仅象征着黛西的出现，也象征着重返纯真青春的希望，重返那个在他被生活失望和腐蚀之前的时光。正如这些例子所表明的那样，虽然失去的欲望对象从字面上讲是我们语言出现之前的幻想中与母亲的结合，但在我们年轻的时候，可能会发生一些事件，甚至整个时期，我们会无意识地将之与这种幻想结合联系起来，这些事件或时期可以作为这种结合的替代品，因此我们会将它们视为失去的欲望对象。

It is important to note that objet petit a also refers to anything that puts me in touch with my repressed desire for my lost object. For example, when the narrator of Marcel Proust’s Remembrance of Things Past (1913) tastes for the first time since childhood a small teacake called a madeleine, he experiences a joyful regression to his early youth. He is flooded with unexpected and vivid memories. For him, the madeleine is objet petit a. For The Great Gatsby’s Jay Gatsby, perhaps the green light at the end of Daisy’s dock is objet petit a, for one might argue that the light holds for Gatsby not just the promise of Daisy, but the promise of a return to his innocent youth, a return to a time before he was disappointed and corrupted by life. As these examples illustrate, although the lost object of desire is, literally, our preverbal fantasy union with our mother, there can be events or even whole periods of time later in our youth that we unconsciously associate with that fantasy union, that are stand-ins for it, and that we therefore respond to as lost objects of desire.

在拉康精神分析中，丧失和匮乏的重要性怎么强调都不为过。事实上，语言的使用本身就蕴含着一种丧失和匮乏，因为如果我仍然觉得自己与事物密不可分，我就不需要用词语来指代它们。例如，我需要用“毯子”这个词来指代我的毯子，正是因为我不再拥有过去对毯子的体验。如果我仍然觉得我的毯子和我融为一体，仍然是同一事物，我就不需要用“毯子”这个词来指代它。因此，象征秩序，或者说通过语言所知的世界，引向了匮乏的世界。我不再与我的毯子、我的母亲、我的世界融为一体。所以我需要词语来表达我对这些事物的概念。

The importance of loss and lack in Lacanian psychoanalysis cannot be stressed too strongly. The use of language in general, in fact, implies a loss, a lack, because I wouldn’t need words as stand-ins for things if I still felt that I was an inseparable part of those things. For example, I need the word blanket as a stand-in for my blanket precisely because I no longer have my former experience of my blanket. If I felt that my blanket and myself were still in union, were still one and the same thing, I wouldn’t need the word blanket to refer to it. Thus, the Symbolic Order, or the world known through language, ushers in the world of lack. I am no longer one with my blanket, my mother, my world. So I need words to represent my concepts of these things.

此外，由于刚才描述的匮乏体验，象征秩序标志着意识和无意识的分裂。事实上，无意识源于我们最初对与母亲结合的渴望的压抑，这种渴望在我们感受到象征秩序出现之前就已经存在。因为我们所经历的匮乏被压抑了——我们难以承受的失落感、我们受挫的渴望、我们因拥有某些渴望而产生的内疚感，以及伴随如此巨大损失而来的恐惧——正如我们在本章前面所了解到的，正是压抑……首先，它创造了无意识。事实上，拉康那句著名的论断——“无意识的结构就像一种语言”（《研讨会》，第七卷，第12页）——暗示着，无意识的欲望总是在寻找我们失去的欲望对象，寻找我们语言前经验中的幻想之母，正如语言总是在寻找用语言来表达我们成年后所栖居的客体世界的方法一样，而当我们还是语言前婴儿时，我们与这些客体融为一体，它们并不需要语言来表达。

In addition, the Symbolic Order, as a result of the experience of lack just described, marks the split into conscious and unconscious mind. In fact, the unconscious is created by our initial repression of our desire for the union with our mother we felt we had prior to the advent of the Symbolic Order. For the lack we experienced was repressed – our overwhelming sense of loss, our frustrated desire, our guilt over having certain kinds of desire, and the fears that accompany a loss of such magnitude – and as we learned earlier in this chapter, it is repression that first creates the unconscious. Indeed, Lacan’s famous statement that “the unconscious is structured like a language” (Seminar, Bk. VII 12) implies, among other things, the way in which unconscious desire is always seeking our lost object of desire, the fantasy mother of our preverbal experience, just as language is always seeking ways to put into words the world of objects we inhabit as adults, objects that didn’t need words when we felt, as preverbal infants, one with them.

无意识的结构也以另一种方式类似于语言，这种方式涉及丧失或缺失。拉康认为，无意识的运作类似于语言中两种非常常见的过程，这两种过程都暗示着某种丧失或缺失：隐喻和转喻。请耐心听我说。这个论证比你想象的要生动有趣得多。隐喻出现在语言中，指用一个对象来代表另一个截然不同的对象，但我们仍然想将两者进行比较。例如，如果我想表达尽管我的爱与它明显不同，但它却拥有红玫瑰的特质：惊艳的美丽、柔软的触感、能够伤害我的能力（毕竟玫瑰有刺），等等，那么一朵红玫瑰就可以成为我爱的隐喻。转喻出现在语言中，指用一个与另一个对象相关或属于另一个对象一部分的对象来代表整个对象。例如，我可能会说“我认为王冠应该表现得更好”，以此表明我不赞同国王的某些行为，这里用王冠来指代国王，因为它与国王密切相关。请注意，隐喻和转喻都包含一种缺失，一种损失或不足：它们都代表着某种被搁置的事物。玫瑰的特质和王冠的功能在这里被暂时凸显出来：隐喻和转喻本身占据了舞台，而不是它们所代表的个体。

The unconscious is also structured like a language in another way that involves loss or lack. For Lacan argues that the operations of the unconscious resemble two very common processes of language that imply a kind of loss or lack: metaphor and metonymy. Now stay with me here. This argument is less dry and more clever than you might expect. Metaphors occur in language when one object is used as a standin for another, dissimilar object to which we want to nevertheless compare it. A red rose, for example, can be a metaphor for my love if I want to suggest that, despite their obvious dissimilarities, my love has the qualities of a red rose: striking beauty, softness to the touch, the ability to hurt me (a rose has thorns, after all), and so forth. Metonymy occurs in language when an object associated with or part of another object is used as a stand-in for the whole object. For instance, I might say, “I think the crown should be expected to behave better” to indicate that I do not approve of something the king has done, with crown as the metonym for king because it is associated with the latter. Note that both metaphor and metonymy involve an absence, a kind of loss or lack: they’re both stand-ins for something being pushed aside, so to speak. The qualities of the rose and the function of the crown are momentarily foregrounded here: the metaphor and the metonym occupy the stage, not the individuals whom these figures of speech represent.

拉康指出，隐喻类似于一种被称为凝缩的无意识过程，因为两者都将不相似的事物联系起来。正如本章前面“梦与梦的象征”一节所述，凝缩是指我们用一个人或一个物体来替代几个不同的人或物体，从而将它们“联系起来”。例如，我可能梦见自己被一头饥饿的狮子追赶，而实际上是我的债主、心怀不满的配偶和不满的老板让我心烦意乱。类似地，转喻类似于一种无意识的置换过程，因为两者都用一个人或物体来替代另一个与前者在某种程度上相关的人或物体。正如前面“防御机制、焦虑与核心问题”和“梦与梦的象征”两节所述，置换是指我们用一个威胁性较小的人或​​物体来替代真正让我们感到痛苦的人或物体。例如，我可能会对我的孩子（一个“下属”）大吼大叫，而实际上我生气的对象是我的雇主（一个我“下属”的人）。

Metaphor, Lacan observes, is akin to the unconscious process called condensation because both processes bring dissimilar things together. As mentioned earlier in this chapter, in the section entitled “Dreams and Dream Symbols,” condensation occurs when we substitute a person or object for several dissimilar persons or objects, which are thus “brought together.” For example, I might dream I am being pursued by a hungry lion when it is actually my creditors, my disgruntled spouse, and my dissatisfied employer that are all upsetting me. Analogously, metonymy is akin to the unconscious process of displacement because both processes substitute a person or object for another person or object with which the first is, in some way, associated. As described in the previous sections entitled “The Defenses, Anxiety, and Core Issues” and “Dreams and Dream Symbols,” displacement occurs when we substitute a less threatening person or object for the person or object that is actually distressing us. For instance, I might yell at my child (someone who is “under” me) when it is actually my employer (someone I am “under”) with whom I’m angry.

在所有这些无意识结构如同语言的例子中，请注意，关键要素是丧失或匮乏。在我们最近的例子中……隐喻和转喻，总是用一件事物来替代另一件被边缘化的事物。在我们之前的例子——用语言徒劳地试图重新建立我们前语言时代与世界合一的感觉——中，某种失去的东西总是被追寻，却永远无法寻回。因此，当我们进入象征秩序——语言的世界——时，我们也进入了一个充满失落和匮乏的世界。我们已经离开了想象秩序，那个我们曾拥有满足感和掌控感的世界。如今，我们生活在一个他人拥有需求、欲望和恐惧的世界，这些限制了我们关注自身需求、欲望和恐惧的方式和程度。这里不再有持续满足的幻觉，也不再有完全掌控的安慰性幻想。在这个新世界里，我们必须遵守规则，必须服从限制。

In all of these examples of the ways in which the unconscious is structured like a language, note that the key ingredient is loss or lack. In our recent examples of metaphor and metonymy, one thing is always being substituted for another that gets pushed into the background. In our earlier example – of the use of words as a vain effort to reconnect with our pre-verbal feeling of union with our world – something lost is always being pursued but is never found. Thus, in entering the Symbolic Order – the world of language – we’re entering a world of loss and lack. We’ve exited the Imaginary Order, the world in which we had the illusion of fulfillment and control. We now inhabit a world in which others have needs, desires, and fears that limit the ways in which and the extent to which we can attend to our own needs, desires, and fears. There is no more illusion of sustained fulfillment here, no more comforting fantasy of complete control. This new world is one in which there are rules we must obey and restrictions by which we must abide.

根据拉康的理论，第一条规则是：母亲属于父亲，而非属于我。至少对小男孩来说，这种进入象征秩序的启蒙，正是弗洛伊德所说的俄狄浦斯情结。小男孩必须找到母亲的替代品，因为她不再只属于他。事实上，因为她属于父亲，她就完全不再属于小男孩了。因此，拉康认为象征秩序标志着对母亲的欲望被“父亲之名”所取代，也就不足为奇了。因为我们正是通过语言被社会化，通过语言学习社会规则和禁忌，而这些规则和禁忌过去是、现在仍然是由父亲制定的，也就是由过去和现在拥有权威的男性制定的。的确，阳具（阴茎的象征，因此也是父权制权力的隐喻）具有讽刺意味地蕴含着完全权力的承诺，但它同时也是匮乏的象征，因为它象征着象征秩序。拉康对“父之名”（法语中，“父之名”是 Nom -d​​u-Père，这是对Non – 或No – du Père 的双关语，意为“没有”的父亲）的双关，强调了象征秩序的限制性维度。

The first rule, according to Lacan, is the rule that Mother belongs to Father and not to me. For little boys, at least, this initiation into the Symbolic Order is what Freud calls the oedipal prohibition. Junior must find substitutes for Mother because she is no longer his alone. In fact, because she is Father’s, she is no longer Junior’s at all. It should come as no surprise, then, that Lacan says the Symbolic Order marks the replacement of the Desire of the Mother with the Name-of-the-Father. For it is through language that we are socially programmed, that we learn the rules and prohibitions of our society, and those rules and prohibitions were and still are authored by the Father, that is, by men in authority past and present. Indeed, the phallus (the symbolic equivalent of the penis and therefore a metaphor for patriarchal power) ironically holds the promise of complete power yet is the sign of lack because it is the sign of the Symbolic Order. And Lacan’s pun on the Name-of-the-Father (in French, the Name-of-the-Father is the Nom-du-Père, which is a pun on the Non – or No – du Père: the “No”-of-the-Father) underscores the restrictive dimension of the Symbolic Order.

事实上，象征秩序在我们所谓“自我”的形成过程中扮演着如此重要的角色，以至于我们并非我们自认为的那样独特、独立。我们的欲望、信念、偏见等等，都是在我们沉浸于象征秩序的过程中被建构出来的，尤其当我们的父母引导我们沉浸其中，并受到他们自身对象征秩序的反应的影响时，这种沉浸感更是被塑造。这正是拉康所说的“欲望总是他者的欲望”（《研讨会》，第十一卷，第235页）的含义。我们或许认为，我们对生活的追求，甚至在任何特定时刻的渴望，都源于我们独特的个性、意志和判断。然而，我们所渴望的，实际上是我们被教导去渴望的。如果我们成长于不同的文化——也就是不同的象征秩序——我们就会拥有不同的欲望。换言之，象征秩序由社会的意识形态构成：它的信念、价值观和偏见；它包括政府体制、法律、教育实践、宗教信条等等。正是我们对社会意识形态的回应塑造了我们。这就是拉康在讨论象征秩序时将“他者”一词大写的含义。他者 指的是任何有助于形成我们主体性或我们通常所说的“自我”的事物：例如，符号秩序、语言、意识形态——它们实际上是同义词——或者任何权威人物或公认的社会习俗。

So enormous is the role of the Symbolic Order in the formation of what we refer to as our “selves,” in fact, that we are not the unique, independent individuals we think we are. Our desires, beliefs, biases, and so forth are constructed for us as a result of our immersion in the Symbolic Order, especially as that immersion is carried out by our parents and influenced by their own responses to the Symbolic Order. This is what Lacan means by his claim that “desire is always the desire of the Other” (Seminar, Bk. XI 235). We may think that what we want out of life, or even what we want at any given moment, is the result of our own unique personalities, our own wills and judgments. However, what we desire is what we are taught to desire. If we were raised in a different culture – that is, in a different Symbolic Order – we would have different desires. In other words, the Symbolic Order consists of society’s ideologies: its beliefs, values, and biases; its system of government, laws, educational practices, religious tenets, and the like. And it is our responses to our society’s ideologies that make us who we are. This is what Lacan means when he capitalizes the word other when discussing the Symbolic Order. Other refers to anything that contributes to the creation of our subjectivity, or what we commonly refer to as our “selfhood”: for example, the Symbolic Order, language, ideology – which are virtually synonymous – or any authority figure or accepted social practice.

然而，值得注意的是，当我们压抑或潜意识化我们对前语言时代童年世界的渴望——那个我们曾幻想拥有圆满和掌控的世界，那个我们相信母亲只为我们而活的世界——我们并非压抑想象秩序。相反，即使象征秩序占据主导地位，想象秩序仍然存在于意识的背景之中。象征秩序主宰着人类文化和社会秩序，因为仅仅停留在想象秩序中就意味着无法在社会中正常运作。尽管如此，想象秩序仍然会通过象征秩序所归类为误解、误读或感知错误的体验而显现出来。也就是说，任何不符合构成象征秩序的社会规范和期望的体验或观点，都会让想象秩序显现出来。然而，从这个意义上讲，想象秩序也是创造力的沃土，没有它，我们或许无法将自身视为完整的人。甚至可以说，想象秩序的深刻价值恰恰在于它不像象征秩序那样控制我们的生活。具有讽刺意味的是，正是这种控制的“缺失”，或许为我们提供了对抗构成象征秩序的意识形态体系的唯一力量。尽管如此，拉康认为，象征秩序和想象秩序都试图控制或逃避他所谓的“实在界”。

It is important to note, however, that in repressing, in rendering unconscious, our desire for the world of our preverbal childhood – the world in which we had the illusion of fulfillment and control, the world in which we believed Mother lived for us alone – we are not repressing the Imaginary Order. Rather, the Imaginary Order continues to exist in the background of consciousness even as the Symbolic Order holds sway in the foreground. The Symbolic Order dominates human culture and social order, for to remain solely in the Imaginary Order is to render oneself incapable of functioning in society. Nevertheless, the Imaginary Order makes itself felt through experiences of the kind the Symbolic Order would classify as misinterpretations, misunderstandings, or errors of perception. That is, the Imaginary Order makes itself felt through any experience or viewpoint that does not conform adequately to the societal norms and expectations that constitute the Symbolic Order. Yet in this capacity, the Imaginary Order is also a fertile source of creativity without which we probably wouldn’t recognize ourselves as fully human. One might even argue that the profound value of the Imaginary Order lies in the very fact of its not controlling our lives the way the Symbolic Order does. Ironically, it is this “lack” of control that probably offers us the only resistance we have to the ideological systems that constitute the Symbolic Order. Nevertheless, Lacan posits that both the Symbolic and the Imaginary Orders attempt to control or avoid what he calls the Real.

拉康的“实在界”概念非常晦涩难懂，他自己也难以解释清楚。我们可以这样理解“实在界”：它超越了我们所有意义建构体系，存在于社会用来解释存在的意识形态所构建的世界之外。也就是说，“实在界”是存在的不可解释的维度；它是脱离了我们意义建构体系的过滤和缓冲的存在。例如，“实在界”就是我们有时会有的体验，即使只是短暂的一瞬，当我们感到生命没有目的或意义，当我们怀疑支配社会的宗教和世俗价值观是骗局、错误或是偶然的结果时。换句话说，当我们看穿意识形态，意识到正是意识形态——而非某些永恒的价值观或真理——塑造了我们所知的世界时，我们就体验到了“实在界”。我们感觉到，意识形态就像一幅绣满我们整个世界的帷幕，而我们知道，帷幕之后便是“实在界”。但我们无法看清帷幕后的真相。“实在界”是我们一无所知的，只能时不时地感到它的存在，并为此感到焦虑。这就是拉康将这种体验称为“实在界创伤”的原因。它让我们感到恐惧，因为它告诉我们，社会为我们创造的意义并非真实存在。仅此而已——社会的产物——但它却无法取代那些原本的意义。真实世界的创伤仅仅让我们意识到，隐藏在社会意识形态之下的现实，是我们无法认知和解释的现实，因此也绝对超出了我们的掌控能力。

Lacan’s notion of the Real is a very difficult concept that he had trouble explaining. One way to think of the Real is as that which is beyond all our meaning-making systems, that which lies outside the world created by the ideologies society uses to explain existence. That is, the Real is the uninterpretable dimension of existence; it is existence without the filters and buffers of our signifying, or meaning-making, systems. For example, the Real is that experience we have, perhaps on a daily basis even if it’s only for a moment, when we feel that there is no purpose or meaning to life, when we suspect that the religious and secular values governing society are hoaxes or mistakes or the results of chance. In other words, we experience the Real when we have a moment in which we see through ideology, when we realize that it is ideology – and not some set of timeless values or eternal truths – that has made the world as we know it. We sense that ideology is like a curtain upon which our whole world is embroidered, and we know that behind that curtain is the Real. But we can’t see behind the curtain. The Real is something we can know nothing about, except to have the anxious feeling from time to time that it’s there. That’s why Lacan calls this kind of experience the trauma of the Real. It terrifies us because it tells us that the meanings society has created for us are just that – the creations of society – but it gives us nothing in place of those meanings. The trauma of the Real gives us only the realization that the reality hidden beneath the ideologies society has created is a reality beyond our capacity to know and explain and therefore certainly beyond our capacity to control.

好了，如果你坚持读到这里，你肯定会问：“这一切和文学阐释有什么关系呢？”鉴于拉康式文学阐释与我们在本章其余部分讨论的更为标准的、或经典的精神分析文学阐释方法截然不同，或许最好先大致了解一下拉康式文学批评家所做的文学分析类型。我们的目标并非让你自己进行拉康式分析，而是让你熟悉这种阐释方法，以便你在阅读拉康式文学阐释时更加得心应手，并在准备就绪后尝试自己进行阐释。

Okay, if you’ve hung on this far, you must be asking, “What does all this have to do with literary interpretation?” Given that Lacanian literary interpretation is quite different from the more standard, or classical, psychoanalytic approach to literature that we address in the rest of this chapter, it might be a good idea just to become generally acquainted with the kinds of literary analysis done by Lacanian literary critics. Our goal here is not to enable you to do a Lacanian analysis yourself but simply to familiarize you with this kind of interpretation so that you’ll be more comfortable and knowledgeable when you read Lacanian literary interpretations and, when you’re ready, try one yourself.

或许，运用拉康视角解读文学作品最可靠的方法，尤其是在初次尝试这种方法时，是探索文本如何受到我们刚才讨论的一些关键拉康概念的影响，并观察这种探索能揭示什么。例如，叙事中的人物、事件或情节是否体现了想象秩序？如果是，它们是否涉及某种私人的、幻想的或妄想的世界？文本的哪些部分似乎受到象征秩序的影响？也就是说，我们在哪里可以看到意识形态和社会规范控制着人物的行为和叙事事件？这两种秩序之间的关系是如何被描绘的？如果我们能够发现人物将他们对“小客体a”（objet petit a）的无意识欲望寄托于何处，我们又能了解到关于人物的哪些信息？换句话说，某个人物将他或她对萦绕心头、理想化的婴儿母亲的无意识欲望放置（或者更准确地说，转移）于何处？文本的任何部分是否似乎代表了真实，代表了存在的那个维度，那个维度如此可怕地超出了我们的理解能力，以至于我们的本能是逃避它、压制它和否认它？

Perhaps the most reliable way to interpret a literary work through a Lacanian lens, especially when you first try the approach, is to explore the ways in which the text might be structured by some of the key Lacanian concepts we’ve just discussed and see what this exploration can reveal. For example, do any characters, events, or episodes in the narrative seem to embody the Imaginary Order, in which case they would involve some kind of private and either fantasy or delusional world? What parts of the text seem informed by the Symbolic Order? That is, where do we see ideology and social norms in control of characters’ behavior and narrative events? How is the relationship between these two orders portrayed? What do we learn about characters if we can discover where they’ve invested their unconscious desire for objet petit a? In other words, where has a given character placed (or displaced, to be more precise) his or her unconscious desire for the haunting, idealized mother of infancy? Does any part of the text seem to operate as a representative of the Real, of that dimension of existence that remains so terrifyingly beyond our ability to comprehend it that our impulse is to flee it, to repress and deny it?

让我们简要地来看两个文学例子。首先，我相信你们很多人都读过夏洛特·珀金斯·吉尔曼那篇经常被收入选集的短篇小说《黄色壁纸》（1892）。我们如何才能说，故事中那位没有名字的叙述者在想象界停留的时间越来越长，直到她实际上完全生活在其中？她对想象界的诉求是如何构成对象征界的拒绝的？象征界显然体现在她的丈夫和兄弟身上。壁纸又如何被视为拉康式实在界的象征？叙述者与壁纸的遭遇又是如何展现实在界带来的创伤的？我们是否可以这样假设，《黄色壁纸》描绘了一个人物陷入拉康式困境的境地：她发现自己被困在两个无法忍受的选择之间——一个是她觉得过于束缚的象征界，另一个是难以理解的实在界？她唯一剩下的位置，她逐渐适应并最终完全占据了，是想象秩序。事实上，故事的结尾是主人公像个幼童一样在房间里爬来爬去，无法作为社会成员正常生活，而拉康理论告诉我们，这总是完全沉浸于想象秩序的结果。

Let’s look briefly at two literary examples. First, I’m sure many of you have read the frequently anthologized story by Charlotte Perkins Gilman entitled “The Yellow Wallpaper” (1892). In what way might we say that the story’s unnamed narrator spends more and more time in the Imaginary Order until she, in effect, lives there entirely? How is her recourse to the Imaginary Order a rejection of the Symbolic Order, which is evidently embodied in her husband and brother? How might the wallpaper be seen as a representation of the Lacanian Real? How do the narrator’s encounters with the wallpaper illustrate the trauma of the Real? Might we be justified in hypothesizing that “The Yellow Wallpaper” illustrates a situation in which a character finds herself caught between a Lacanian rock and a hard place, so to speak, in that she’s caught between two unlivable alternatives: a Symbolic Order she finds too restrictive and the incomprehensible Real? The only position left her, to which she gradually becomes acclimated and which she finally inhabits entirely, is the Imaginary Order. Indeed, the story ends with the protagonist crawling around the room like a very young child, unable to function as a member of society, which Lacanian theory tells us is always the result of total immersion in the Imaginary Order.

第二个简短的例子，我们来看凯特·肖邦经常被收入选集的短篇小说《觉醒》（1899）。小说的主人公埃德娜·庞特利耶同样被“想象秩序”所吸引：对她而言，想象秩序指的是艺术、音乐、性自由和无拘无束的爱情世界。她之所以被“想象秩序”所吸引，一部分原因是她对抚养她长大的情感疏离的父亲和姐姐的反感，另一部分原因是她的丈夫莱昂斯，他完全沉浸在“象征秩序”之中，几乎成了其代言人。然而，埃德娜被“想象秩序”所吸引，也是为了寻找某种她无法辨识的东西。她被一种无法满足的渴望所困扰，这种渴望无法被她的艺术所满足，无法被赖兹小姐的音乐所满足，无法被她自身的性自由所满足，也无法被爱情所满足。拉康式的读者或许会说，埃德娜始终无法满足，是因为她没有意识到艺术、音乐、性自由和浪漫爱情都只是她对“小客体a”（objet petit a）的替代品。“小客体a”是她幼年时与母亲/她所处的世界建立的幻想性结合，而这种结合在她潜意识中依然存在。事实上，我们或许可以认为，正是这种潜意识欲望的力量，最终将她赤裸如初地拉入与大海的致命结合之中。在那里，她最后的体验是感官的，而非语言的，是她青春的记忆：她听到狗吠声、马刺的叮当声、蜜蜂的嗡嗡声，闻到花香。因此，就埃德娜的经历而言，我们可以合理地假设，《觉醒》的结构是由主人公潜意识中对“小客体a”的追寻所构成的，而这种追寻必然是徒劳的，因为“小客体a”永远是一个永远无法寻回的遗失之物。

For our second brief example, let’s try Kate Chopin’s frequently anthologized novella The Awakening (1899). Here again, we have a female protagonist, Edna Pontellier, who is drawn to the Imaginary Order: in her case, the world of art, music, sexual freedom, and unfettered romance. She is drawn to the Imaginary Order partly in response to the emotionally distant father and older sister who raised her and partly in response to her husband Léonce, who is so thoroughly bound to the Symbolic Order that he is practically its poster child. However, Edna is also drawn to the Imaginary Order in search of something she can’t identify. She is haunted by a longing that can’t be satisfied, not by her art, not by Mademoiselle Reisz’s music, not by her own sexual freedom, and not by romance. A Lacanian reader might say that Edna remains unsatisfied because she doesn’t realize that art, music, sexual freedom, and romance are just her substitutes for objet petit a, the fantasy union with her mother/her world she experienced in infancy and still unconsciously desires. Indeed, we might argue that it is the strength of this unconscious desire that finally draws her, as naked as the day she was born, into her fatal union with the sea, where her last experiences are sensory, not verbal, memories of her youth: she hears the barking of a dog, the clanging of spurs, the hum of bees, and she smells the odor of flowers. In terms of Edna’s experience, then, we might be justified in hypothesizing that The Awakening is structured by the protagonist’s unconscious search for objet petit a, a search that is necessarily unsuccessful, for objet petit a is always a lost object that can never be found.

拉康精神分析运用了大量的概念，其复杂程度远非这篇简短概述所能涵盖。尽管如此，即使是这几个理论概念和文学例证，也能让我们初步了解拉康对人类经验的独特视角，以及他对文学的独到见解。

Lacanian psychoanalysis employs many more concepts and is much more complex than a brief summary like this can convey. Nevertheless, even these few theoretical concepts and literary examples can allow us to begin to understand the unique perspective on human experience and the interesting insights into literature Lacan offers us.

古典精神分析与文学

Classical psychoanalysis and literature

当然，经典精神分析的概念远不止我们之前讨论的这些。如同其他领域一样，经典精神分析理论家之间也存在诸多分歧，例如，人格的形成方式以及治疗功能失调行为的最佳方法。在精神分析文学批评家之间，对于如何将精神分析概念应用于文学研究也存在诸多争议。一位作家的文学作品在对其人生进行精神分析时应该扮演怎样的角色？在多大程度上，我们可以像分析真实人物一样分析文学作品中的人物？读者究竟扮演着怎样的角色？在阅读文本的过程中，哪些精神分析理论家能提供最深刻的见解？读者通过将自身的欲望和冲突投射到作品上，在“创造”文本的过程中又扮演着怎样的角色？正如您在第六章“读者反应批评”中所见，精神分析和读者反应理论在关注读者心理体验方面存在诸多重叠之处。在第三章和第四章中，我们还将看到精神分析与马克思主义和女权主义的一些重叠之处，以及马克思主义和女权主义在某些方面对精神分析视角的否定。然而，我们目前的目的仅仅是概述精神分析的主要思想和基本原则，这些原则与大多数其他精神分析概念在某种程度上都有关联，以便您能够更好地理解精神分析理论家和文学批评家提出的问题，从而更有效地阅读他们的著作。

Of course, there are also many more concepts in classical psychoanalysis than the ones discussed earlier. And as in every field, there is a good deal of disagreement among classical psychoanalytic theorists concerning, for example, the ways in which our personalities are formed and the best ways of treating dysfunctional behavior. Among psychoanalytic literary critics, there is much disagreement concerning how psychoanalytic concepts can best be applied to our study of literature. What role should an author’s literary output play in our psychoanalysis of his or her life? To what extent is it legitimate to psychoanalyze literary characters as if they were real people? When doing so, which psychoanalytic theorists offer us the best insights? What role do readers play in “creating” the text they’re reading by projecting their own desires and conflicts onto the work? As you’ll see when you read Chapter 6 on reader-response criticism, psychoanalysis and reader-response theory overlap in many ways concerning their attention to the psychological experience of the reader. We’ll also see in Chapters 3 and 4 some overlap of psychoanalysis with Marxism and feminism as well as some ways in which Marxism and feminism reject the psychoanalytic perspective. Our purpose at this point, however, is simply to cover the main ideas, the basic principles of psychoanalysis to which most other psychoanalytic concepts are in some way related in order to facilitate your reading of psychoanalytic theorists and literary critics with some understanding of the issues they raise.

显而易见，我们讨论过的所有精神分析概念不可能在每一部文学作品中都得到体现。当我们进行精神分析阅读时，我们的任务是找出文本中哪些概念以某种方式发挥作用，从而加深我们对作品的理解；如果我们打算就此撰写论文，则需要从中得出有意义且连贯的精神分析解释。从经典精神分析理论的视角来看（这也是本章的主要关注点），我们可以重点关注作品中对俄狄浦斯情结或一般家庭动力的呈现；作品能够告诉我们关于人类与死亡或性欲的心理关系；叙述者无意识问题在故事进程中不断显现的方式；或者任何其他似乎有助于我们理解文本的精神分析概念。

It stands to reason that you won’t find every psychoanalytic concept we’ve discussed represented in every literary work you read. Our job, when we read psychoanalytically, is to see which concepts are operating in the text in such a way as to enrich our understanding of the work and, if we plan to write a paper about it, to yield a meaningful, coherent psychoanalytic interpretation. From the perspective of classical psychoanalytic theory, which is our primary focus in this chapter, we might attend mainly to the work’s representation of oedipal dynamics or of family dynamics in general; to what the work can tell us about human beings’ psychological relationship to death or to sexuality; to the way the narrator’s unconscious problems keep asserting themselves over the course of the story; or to any other psychoanalytic concepts that seem to produce a useful understanding of the text.

一些批评家反对运用精神分析来理解文学人物的行为，因为文学人物并非真实存在的人，因此不具备可供分析的心理。然而，对文学人物的行为进行精神分析或许是学习如何运用这一理论的最佳途径。此外，许多精神分析批评家从两个重要方面捍卫了这种做法：（1）当我们对文学人物进行精神分析时，我们并非认为他们是真实存在的人，而是认为他们代表了人类普遍的心理体验；（2）对文学人物的行为进行精神分析，与从女性主义、马克思主义或非裔美国人批评视角，或从任何将文学表征视为现实生活问题例证的批评理论视角来分析他们的行为一样合理。

Some critics have objected to the use of psychoanalysis to understand the behavior of literary characters because literary characters are not real people and, therefore, do not have psyches that can be analyzed. However, psychoanalyzing the behavior of literary characters is probably the best way to learn how to use the theory. Furthermore, this practice has been defended by many psychoanalytic critics on two important grounds: (1) when we psychoanalyze literary characters, we are not suggesting that they are real people but that they represent the psychological experience of human beings in general; and (2) it is just as legitimate to psychoanalyze the behavior represented by literary characters as it is to analyze their behavior from a feminist, Marxist, or African American critical perspective, or from the perspective of any critical theory that analyzes literary representations as illustrations of real-life issues.

让我们来看几个具体的例子，了解运用经典精神分析来解读文学人物的行为会产生哪些洞见。对阿瑟·米勒的《推销员之死》（1949）进行精神分析解读，可以考察威利·洛曼对过去的闪回是如何由他当前的心理创伤引发的退行性事件：他自己和儿子们在商业上的失败，以及威利为了缓解这种失败而渴望的成功。他自幼被父亲和哥哥抛弃后，便一直饱受巨大的不安全感折磨。因此，这部剧的结构围绕着被压抑之物的回归展开，因为威利一生都在通过否认和逃避来压抑自己的心理不安全感，以及由此导致的社交障碍和事业失败。从精神分析的角度来看，《推销员之死》或许可以被解读为对家庭心理动力学的探索：它探讨了我们在家庭中未解决的角色冲突如何在职场中“上演”，并“传承”给我们的孩子。

Let’s look at a few specific examples to see the kinds of insights produced by using classical psychoanalysis to interpret the behavior represented by literary characters. A psychoanalytic reading of Arthur Miller’s Death of a Salesman (1949) might examine the ways in which Willy Loman’s flashbacks to the past are really regressive episodes brought on by his present psychological trauma: his own and his sons’ lack of success in the business world, success Willy needed in order to assuage the massive insecurity he’s suffered since his abandonment in childhood by his father and older brother. The play is thus structured by the return of the repressed, for Willy has spent his life repressing, through denial and avoidance, his psychological insecurity and the social inadequacy and business failure that have resulted. From a psychoanalytic perspective, then, Death of a Salesman might be read as an exploration of the psychological dynamics of the family: an exploration of the ways in which unresolved conflicts about our roles within the family are “played out” in the workplace and “passed down” to our children.

同样，对托妮·莫里森的《最蓝的眼睛》（1970）进行精神分析解读，可以分析小说如何揭示种族主义造成的严重心理影响，尤其当这些影响被受害者内化时，例如，许多黑人角色都认为自己的种族具有白人美国人所赋予的负面特质。这些心理影响显而易见，例如：布里德洛夫一家坚信自己丑陋，仅仅因为他们有非洲人的特征；布里德洛夫太太全心全意地为她工作的白人家庭服务，却忽略了自己的家庭；年轻的黑人男孩无情地欺负佩科拉，只因为她皮肤黝黑，这种自我厌恶体现在他们身上；黑人角色和白人角色都认为肤色较浅的非裔美国女孩莫琳·皮尔在各方面都优于肤色较深的同学。杰拉尔丁无法放松享受生活，也无法让自己去爱她的丈夫和儿子，因为她害怕哪怕最轻微的失控（无论是情绪失控还是头发自然卷曲失控）都会让她变成“黑鬼”，她用这个词来称呼任何不符合她着装和行为标准的黑人。正如这些例子所示，小说展现了内化的种族主义如何导致黑人角色自我厌恶，并将这种自我憎恨投射到其他同族人身上。在许多黑人角色对待佩科拉的方式中，我们看到了这种投射的破坏性表现，佩科拉对蓝眼睛的自我否定式渴望，最鲜明地体现了种族主义的心理破坏性。或者，我们也可以运用精神分析来理解布里德洛夫一家如何展现功能失调家庭的动态，而这种家庭的根源可以追溯到宝琳和乔利年轻时经历的孤立、遗弃和背叛。

Similarly, a psychoanalytic reading of Toni Morrison’s The Bluest Eye (1970) might analyze the ways in which the novel reveals the debilitating psychological effects of racism, especially when these effects are internalized by its victims, which we see in the belief of many of the black characters that their race has the negative qualities ascribed to it by white America. These psychological effects are evident, for example, in the Breedloves’ conviction that they are ugly simply because they have African features; in Mrs. Breedlove’s devotion to the white family for whom she works, while she neglects her own family; in the self-hatred of the young black boys who mercilessly pick on Pecola for having black skin; in the assumption by black characters as well as white that Maureen Peal, a light-skinned African American girl, is superior in every way to her darker-skinned classmates; and in Geraldine’s inability to relax and enjoy her life or let herself love her husband and son because she fears that the slightest loss of control (whether it be the control of her emotions or of her hair’s natural curl) will make her a “nigger,” as she calls any black person who does not conform to her standard of dress and behavior. As these examples illustrate, the novel shows how internalized racism results in self-contempt on the part of the black characters and in a projection of that self-hatred onto other members of their race. We see particularly damaging forms of this projection in much of the black characters’ treatment of Pecola, whose self-negating desire for blue eyes is the most striking illustration of the psychological destructiveness of racism. Or we might use psychoanalysis to understand the ways in which the Breedloves illustrate the dynamics of the dysfunctional family, the roots of which can be seen in Pauline and Cholly’s youthful experiences of isolation, abandonment, and betrayal.

最后，对玛丽·雪莱的《弗兰肯斯坦》 （1818）进行精神分析解读，或许能揭示维克多创造怪物，导致家人和朋友丧命，是如何满足他潜意识中惩罚父母（伊丽莎白显然是他们的替代品）的需求，以及他如何演绎因父母收养伊丽莎白——这个“完美”的孩子——而产生的强烈且未解决的兄妹竞争。维克多完全没有表现出任何正常的童年嫉妒，反而频繁地表达对这个取代他成为父母唯一关注和爱慕对象的新来者的爱，这表明他压抑了被遗弃的感受，而这种感受由于被隐藏在内心深处，所以无法释放。潜意识中的冲突从未得到解决。例如，在维克多的成年生活中，我们可以看到许多未解决冲突的迹象：他长期远离挚爱的家人，包括与他订婚的伊丽莎白；梦境揭示了他将伊丽莎白和已故母亲在心理上融合，并预示了伊丽莎白的死亡；他反复出现高烧引起的精神错乱，这些症状如同梦境一般，其中频繁出现他害怕自己精神失常或坚称自己完全清醒的言论；以及他似乎总能以一种诡异的方式做出恰到好处的举动，从而促成怪物的下一次谋杀。此外，我们或许可以谨慎地推测，小说中对心理遗弃的描写与玛丽·雪莱本人在生活中所经历的遗弃之间是否存在关联：她的母亲在她出生后不久便去世了；她的父亲发现独自抚养孩子对他来说难以承受；而她父亲后来娶的妻子却冷落了玛丽，反而更偏爱她与前妻所生的女儿。

Finally, a psychoanalytic reading of Mary Shelley’s Frankenstein (1818) might reveal the ways in which Victor’s creation of a monster responsible for the deaths of his family and friends serves his unconscious need to punish his father and mother (for whom Elizabeth is an obvious surrogate) and play out the intense, unresolved sibling rivalry created by their adoption of Elizabeth, the “perfect” child, when Victor was five years old. The total absence of any normal childhood jealousy on Victor’s part, coupled with his frequent protestations of love for the newcomer who dethroned him as the sole object of parental attention and affection, suggest the repression of feelings of abandonment that, because they are kept in the unconscious, are never resolved. We see numerous signs of these unresolved conflicts in Victor’s adult life, for example, in his extremely prolonged absence from his beloved family, including Elizabeth, to whom he is betrothed; in the dream sequence that reveals his psychological merger of Elizabeth and his dead mother and foreshadows the former’s death; in his fits of feverish disorientation, which read like dream sequences and include frequent expressions of fear that he is losing his mind or protestations that he is perfectly sane; and in the uncanny way he seems to always make exactly the right move to facilitate the monster’s next murder. Furthermore, we might cautiously speculate on the relationship between the representation of psychological abandonment in the novel and the experiences of abandonment Mary Shelley apparently suffered in her own life: her mother died shortly after Mary was born; her father found single parenthood more than he could handle; and the woman her father subsequently wed neglected Mary in favor of her own daughter by a previous marriage.

这里或许可以稍作停顿，回答一个关于精神分析解读文学作品的常见问题：如果我们在文学文本中发现精神分析概念，是否意味着作者有意将它们融入其中？如果作者生活在弗洛伊德之前，甚至从未听说过他，又如何能将它们融入文本呢？答案很简单：弗洛伊德并非精神分析原理的发明者；他只是发现了这些原理在人类身上的运作。换句话说，弗洛伊德命名并解释了人类行为的原理，而这些原理在他发现它们之前早已存在，即便他没有描述它们，这些原理也依然存在。因此，任何准确描述人类行为或源于作者无意识的文学作品（我们假定所有创作作品在某种程度上都是如此），都包含精神分析原理，无论作者在创作时是否意识到这些原理的存在。对于精神分析而言，文学，乃至所有艺术形式，在很大程度上都是作者、读者，或者，正如一些当代精神分析批评家所言，我们整个社会中无意识力量运作的产物。

This might be a good place to pause and answer a frequently asked question concerning psychoanalytic readings of literary works: if we find psychoanalytic concepts operating in a literary text, does it mean that the author has deliberately put them there, and how can an author put them there if he or she lived before Freud or never heard of him? The answer is simple: Freud didn’t invent psychoanalytic principles; he discovered them operating in human beings. In other words, Freud named and explained principles of human behavior that were present long before he found them and that would be present even if he hadn’t described them. So any literary text that accurately describes human behavior or that is the product of an author’s unconscious (which we presume all creative works are to some extent) will include psychoanalytic principles whether or not the author had any awareness of those principles when writing the work. For psychoanalysis, literature, and indeed all art forms, are largely products of unconscious forces at work in the author, in the reader, or, for some contemporary psychoanalytic critics, in our society as a whole.

我们对精神分析概念的运用并不局限于单一文学体裁或艺术媒介；我们可以运用精神分析批评来解读小说、诗歌、戏剧、民间传说和非虚构作品，也可以用它来诠释绘画、雕塑、建筑、电影和音乐。任何涉及图像、看似具有叙事内容（例如许多绘画作品似乎在讲述故事）或与创作者或使用者心理相关的作品（几乎涵盖一切！）都可以运用精神分析工具进行解读。

Our use of psychoanalytic concepts is not limited to one literary genre or to one artistic medium; we can use psychoanalytic criticism to read works of fiction, poetry, drama, folklore, and nonfiction, and we can use it to interpret paintings, sculptures, architecture, films, and music. Any human production that involves images, that seems to have narrative content (the way many paintings seem to tell a story), or that relates to the psychology of those who produce or use it (which means just about everything!) can be interpreted using psychoanalytic tools.

精神分析批评家们对文学文本提出的一些问题

Some questions psychoanalytic critics ask about literary texts

以下问题旨在概括精神分析在文学研究中的应用。无论采用何种方法，通常都需要指出精神分析的本质在于……你所分析的文本维度有助于推动叙事（对情节发展起着至关重要的作用）。问题7提供了一种独特的拉康式文学分析方法。

The following questions are offered to summarize psychoanalytic approaches to literature. Whatever approach you use, it is customary to note that the psychoanalytic dimension of the text you examine helps drive the narrative (is responsible for a good deal of the plot). Question 7 offers a specifically Lacanian approach to literature.

1压抑机制如何构建或影响作品？也就是说，主人公（们）的潜意识动机是什么？由此揭示了哪些核心问题？这些核心问题又如何构建或影响作品？（请记住，潜意识包含被压抑的创伤、恐惧、未解决的冲突和罪恶的欲望。）
